_link.title: I can apply Newton's third law to the electric forces between two charges

toLevel2.question: Charge A (+6 μC) and charge B (+2 μC) are separated by a fixed distance. How does the magnitude of the electric force that A exerts on B compare with the force that B exerts on A?
options: They are equal in magnitude
The force on B is three times larger
The force on A is three times larger
The force on B is six times larger

distractors.answer: The force on B is three times larger
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — students may think the larger charge pushes harder on the smaller one, but Newton's third law guarantees equal magnitudes.

distractors.answer: The force on A is three times larger
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this reverses which charge is supposedly pushed harder; the forces are always equal in magnitude.

distractors.answer: The force on B is six times larger
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this confuses the charge ratio with a force ratio; Newton's third law means both forces have the same magnitude.

toLevel2.question: Newton's third law applied to electric forces states that the two forces in an interaction pair are:
options: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
equal in magnitude and in the same direction
proportional to the charge that experiences them
only equal when the two charges are identical

distractors.answer: equal in magnitude and in the same direction
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the forces act in opposite directions along the line joining the charges.

distractors.answer: proportional to the charge that experiences them
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this contradicts Newton's third law; the magnitudes are always equal regardless of individual charge sizes.

distractors.answer: only equal when the two charges are identical
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law applies regardless of whether the charges are equal or unequal.

toLevel2.question: A proton and an alpha particle (charge +2e) interact electrically. What can be said about the electric force each exerts on the other?
options: Both forces have the same magnitude
The force on the proton is twice as large
The force on the alpha particle is twice as large
The forces depend on which particle is heavier

distractors.answer: The force on the proton is twice as large
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — students may think the larger charge pushes harder on the smaller one, but Newton's third law ensures equal force magnitudes.

distractors.answer: The force on the alpha particle is twice as large
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the charge ratio does not make one force larger; the forces are equal in magnitude.

distractors.answer: The forces depend on which particle is heavier
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the electric force magnitude depends on charges and distance, not mass; and Newton's third law pairs are always equal.

toLevel2.question: Two charged objects exert electric forces on each other. According to Newton's third law, these forces always act:
options: along the line joining the centres of the two charges
perpendicular to the line joining the charges
in the same direction as the electric field
only when both charges are positive

distractors.answer: perpendicular to the line joining the charges
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the Coulomb force acts along the line joining the two charges, not perpendicular to it.

distractors.answer: in the same direction as the electric field
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the third-law pair forces act on different objects and point in opposite directions along the line between them.

distractors.answer: only when both charges are positive
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law applies to all charge combinations, whether both are positive, both negative, or one of each.

toLevel2.question: A small charge of +1 μC is placed near a large charge of +100 μC. Which statement is correct about the electric forces between them?
options: The force on the +1 μC charge equals the force on the +100 μC charge in magnitude
The +100 μC charge exerts 100 times more force on the +1 μC charge
The +1 μC charge exerts no force on the +100 μC charge
The larger charge exerts a stronger force because it has more charge

distractors.answer: The +100 μC charge exerts 100 times more force on the +1 μC charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — students confuse charge ratio with force ratio; Newton's third law means the forces are equal in magnitude.

distractors.answer: The +1 μC charge exerts no force on the +100 μC charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — every charge that experiences a force also exerts an equal and opposite force on the other charge.

distractors.answer: The larger charge exerts a stronger force because it has more charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — although the larger charge contributes to a larger product q₁q₂, both charges experience the same magnitude of force.

toLevel2.question: According to Newton's third law, if charge A exerts a force of 5 N to the right on charge B, then charge B exerts a force of {{blank:1}} on charge A directed to the {{blank:2}}.
The electric forces between two charges form a Newton's third law pair: they are equal in {{blank:1}} and opposite in {{blank:2}}.
Newton's third law applies to the electric force between two charges regardless of the {{blank:1}} of each charge. The forces always act along the {{blank:2}} joining the two charges.
If a +5 μC charge exerts a 2 N force on a −1 μC charge, then the −1 μC charge exerts a 2 N force back on the +5 μC charge.

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law guarantees that the forces are equal in magnitude regardless of the sizes or signs of the charges.

toLevel2.question: A larger charge always exerts a greater electric force on a smaller charge than the smaller charge exerts on the larger charge.

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this is a common misconception; Newton's third law states the forces are always equal in magnitude, regardless of charge size.

toLevel3.question: Charge A (+8 μC) and charge B (+2 μC) are separated by 0.1 m. What is the magnitude of the force that B exerts on A?

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this divides the correct answer by 4, as if only the smaller charge matters; F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9×10⁹ × 8×10⁻⁶ × 2×10⁻⁶ / 0.01 = 14.4 N for both charges.
Incorrect — this multiplies the correct answer by 4, perhaps using the larger charge twice; both forces equal 14.4 N.
Incorrect — this uses only the smaller charge squared; the force on A equals the force on B and is 14.4 N.

toLevel3.question: Two charges, +Q and +4Q, are separated by distance d. A student claims the force on +Q is four times greater than the force on +4Q. Why is this incorrect?
options: Newton's third law requires the forces to be equal in magnitude
The force on the larger charge is actually greater
The forces are equal only when the charges have the same sign
The force depends on distance, not on charge

distractors.answer: The force on the larger charge is actually greater
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this reverses the misconception but is still wrong; Newton's third law pairs are always equal in magnitude.

distractors.answer: The forces are equal only when the charges have the same sign
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law applies to all interactions regardless of the sign of the charges.

distractors.answer: The force depends on distance, not on charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — force depends on both distance and charge, but Newton's third law still ensures both forces are equal in magnitude.

toLevel3.question: Charge X (−3 μC) and charge Y (+9 μC) attract each other with a force of 12 N. If charge X is replaced with a −6 μC charge at the same position, what is the new force on charge Y?
options: 6 N

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — doubling one charge doubles the product q₁q₂ and therefore doubles the force on both charges to 24 N.

distractors.answer: 6 N
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — halving instead of doubling; since q₁ doubled, the force doubles to 24 N for both charges.
Incorrect — this quadruples the force as if both charges were doubled; only one charge doubled so the force doubles to 24 N.

toLevel3.question: A proton and an electron attract each other. The proton has about 1836 times the mass of the electron. How do their accelerations compare?
options: The electron accelerates about 1836 times more than the proton
Both accelerate equally
The proton accelerates more because it has more charge
The proton accelerates about 1836 times more than the electron

distractors.answer: Both accelerate equally
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — while the forces are equal (Newton's third law), the accelerations differ because a = F/m and their masses differ greatly.

distractors.answer: The proton accelerates more because it has more charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — both have the same magnitude of charge (e); the proton accelerates less because it has more mass.

distractors.answer: The proton accelerates about 1836 times more than the electron
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this is backwards; the lighter electron accelerates more for the same force, not the heavier proton.

toLevel3.question: Two charges +Q and −2Q are separated by a distance r. Which statement correctly describes the Newton's third law force pair?
options: Both forces have magnitude kQ(2Q)/r² and point toward the other charge
The force on −2Q is twice the force on +Q
Both forces have magnitude kQ(2Q)/r² but point away from each other
The force on +Q is half the force on −2Q

distractors.answer: The force on −2Q is twice the force on +Q
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law means both forces are equal in magnitude; the charge ratio doesn't make one force bigger.

distractors.answer: Both forces have magnitude kQ(2Q)/r² but point away from each other
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — because the charges are opposite in sign, the forces are attractive and point toward each other, not away.

distractors.answer: The force on +Q is half the force on −2Q
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this is the same misconception as thinking unequal charges produce unequal forces; Newton's third law guarantees equal magnitudes.

toLevel3.question: If you double the charge on one object in a two-charge system, what happens to the force experienced by the other object?
options: It doubles
It stays the same
It quadruples
It halves

distractors.answer: It stays the same
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — F = kq₁q₂/r², so doubling one charge doubles the force on both objects.

distractors.answer: It quadruples
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — quadrupling would require doubling both charges; doubling one charge only doubles the force.

distractors.answer: It halves
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this is the opposite effect; increasing a charge increases the force, not decreases it.

toLevel3.question: Although the electric forces on two unequal charges are equal in magnitude, the {{blank:1}} of the smaller charge is greater because acceleration equals force divided by {{blank:2}}.
When charge A exerts an attractive force on charge B, charge B exerts a force on A that is equal in {{blank:1}} and also {{blank:2}} in nature.
Changing the charge on one object in a pair affects {{blank:1}} forces equally, because Newton's third law requires the forces to remain equal in {{blank:2}}.
If a +2 μC charge and a +8 μC charge interact, the +2 μC charge will accelerate more than the +8 μC charge (assuming equal masses).

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — if the masses are equal and the forces are equal (Newton's third law), then by a = F/m both charges accelerate equally. Unequal acceleration only arises when the masses differ.

toLevel4.question: A +3 μC charge and a +12 μC charge are 0.2 m apart. What is the magnitude of the electric force on the +3 μC charge?

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this uses only the smaller charge squared; F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9×10⁹ × 3×10⁻⁶ × 12×10⁻⁶ / 0.04 = 8.1 N.
Incorrect — this multiplies by 4 as if using the larger charge twice; the correct calculation gives 8.1 N.
Incorrect — this divides by r instead of r²; the correct force is 8.1 N.

toLevel4.question: Two charged spheres A (+5 μC, mass 0.10 kg) and B (−20 μC, mass 0.40 kg) experience an electric force of 8 N. What is the ratio of the acceleration of A to the acceleration of B?

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this is inverted; sphere A has one quarter the mass so it accelerates four times as much: aA/aB = mB/mA = 0.40/0.10 = 4.
Incorrect — equal forces produce equal accelerations only if the masses are equal; here mA < mB so A accelerates more.
Incorrect — this confuses the charge ratio with the acceleration ratio; the acceleration ratio depends on the mass ratio, which is 4 : 1.

toLevel4.question: Charge P (+1 μC) is fixed. Charge Q (+4 μC, mass 2.0 g) is released from rest at a distance where the repulsive force is 0.36 N. What is the initial acceleration of Q?
options: 180 m/s²
720 m/s²
45 m/s²
90 m/s²

distractors.answer: 720 m/s²
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this multiplies by the charge ratio (×4); the force on Q is 0.36 N (Newton's third law), so a = 0.36/0.002 = 180 m/s².

distractors.answer: 45 m/s²
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this divides the force by the charge ratio; the correct acceleration is a = F/m = 0.36/0.002 = 180 m/s².

distractors.answer: 90 m/s²
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this uses a mass of 4.0 g instead of 2.0 g; a = 0.36/0.002 = 180 m/s².

toLevel4.question: Two identical conducting spheres carry charges of +6 μC and +2 μC. They are touched together and then separated to the original distance. How does the new force compare with the original force?
options: The new force is 4/3 times the original force
The new force equals the original force
The new force is half the original force
The new force is double the original force

distractors.answer: The new force equals the original force
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — when touched, charge redistributes equally to +4 μC each; new F ∝ 4×4 = 16, original F ∝ 6×2 = 12, ratio = 16/12 = 4/3.

distractors.answer: The new force is half the original force
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — charge sharing gives +4 μC each; the product 4×4 = 16 is greater than the original 6×2 = 12.

distractors.answer: The new force is double the original force
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the ratio of force products is 16/12 = 4/3, not 2.

toLevel4.question: A −2 μC charge and a +8 μC charge are 0.3 m apart. A student calculates the force on the −2 μC charge as 1.6 N and the force on the +8 μC charge as 6.4 N. What error did the student make?
options: They calculated separate forces using each charge individually instead of using Newton's third law
They forgot to square the distance
They used the wrong value of Coulomb's constant
They added the charges instead of multiplying them

distractors.answer: They forgot to square the distance
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — forgetting to square the distance would give a single wrong answer for both forces, not two different values.

distractors.answer: They used the wrong value of Coulomb's constant
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — using the wrong constant would scale both forces equally, not produce different magnitudes for each charge.

distractors.answer: They added the charges instead of multiplying them
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — adding charges would give a single result; the student's error is treating each charge separately as if it determines its own force.

toLevel4.question: A lithium nucleus (charge +3e, mass 1.2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) and a helium nucleus (charge +2e, mass 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) repel each other with a force of 4.0 × 10⁻¹² N. What is the acceleration of the helium nucleus?
options: 6.1 × 10¹⁴ m/s²
4.1 × 10¹⁴ m/s²
3.3 × 10¹⁴ m/s²
9.1 × 10¹⁴ m/s²

distractors.answer: 4.1 × 10¹⁴ m/s²
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this uses a scaled force based on the charge ratio; both nuclei experience the same 4.0 × 10⁻¹² N force, so a = 4.0×10⁻¹²/6.6×10⁻²⁷ ≈ 6.1×10¹⁴ m/s².

distractors.answer: 3.3 × 10¹⁴ m/s²
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this uses the lithium mass instead of the helium mass; a = F/m = 4.0×10⁻¹²/6.6×10⁻²⁷ ≈ 6.1×10¹⁴ m/s².

distractors.answer: 9.1 × 10¹⁴ m/s²
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this multiplies the force by the charge ratio before dividing by mass; the force on both nuclei is 4.0 × 10⁻¹² N.

toLevel4.question: Charge A exerts a force of 12 N on charge B. If charge A is tripled in magnitude while all else remains constant, what force does B now exert on A?
options: 4 N

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — tripling charge A triples the force on both charges; B exerts the same force on A as A exerts on B, which is now 36 N.

distractors.answer: 4 N
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this divides instead of multiplies by 3; tripling one charge triples the force to 36 N.
Incorrect — this cubes the multiplier instead of simply tripling; the force scales linearly with charge, giving 36 N.

toLevel4.question: Two charges of +Q and +9Q are separated by distance d. The force on each charge is F = k(Q)(9Q)/d² = {{blank:1}}. If +Q has mass m and +9Q has mass 3m, the ratio of their accelerations (a_Q : a_9Q) is {{blank:2}}.
A student says 'the bigger charge pushes harder.' This is {{blank:1}} because Newton's third law guarantees equal {{blank:2}} regardless of charge size.
When a +2 μC charge repels a +6 μC charge with a force of 10 N, the +6 μC charge exerts a force of {{blank:1}} on the +2 μC charge. The direction of this force is {{blank:2}} the +2 μC charge.

toLevel5.question: A +2 μC charge (mass 0.5 g) and a +10 μC charge (mass 5.0 g) are released from rest 0.1 m apart on a frictionless surface. Which statement best describes the subsequent motion?
options: Both accelerate away from each other, with the lighter charge gaining greater speed
Both accelerate away from each other with equal speeds
Only the smaller charge accelerates; the larger one stays still
The larger charge accelerates more because it has more charge

distractors.answer: Both accelerate away from each other with equal speeds
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — equal forces produce unequal accelerations when masses differ; the lighter charge accelerates more and gains greater speed.

distractors.answer: Only the smaller charge accelerates; the larger one stays still
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law means both charges experience a force and therefore both accelerate.

distractors.answer: The larger charge accelerates more because it has more charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — acceleration depends on force and mass (a = F/m); with equal forces, the lighter charge accelerates more.

toLevel5.question: Two charges +Q and +4Q are fixed at separation d. A third charge is placed between them at the point where it experiences zero net force. How does the force the third charge exerts on +Q compare with the force it exerts on +4Q?
options: The force on +Q is one quarter of the force on +4Q
The forces are equal because of Newton's third law
The force on +Q is four times the force on +4Q
The third charge exerts no force on either fixed charge

distractors.answer: The forces are equal because of Newton's third law
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law applies to each pair separately; the third charge is closer to +Q and has a different distance to +4Q, so the forces on +Q and +4Q are different.

distractors.answer: The force on +Q is four times the force on +4Q
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this reverses the relationship; at the zero-force point the third charge is closer to +Q, making the force on +Q smaller (closer but smaller charge), and by Newton's third law each pair has equal forces.

distractors.answer: The third charge exerts no force on either fixed charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the net force on the third charge is zero, but it still exerts individual forces on each fixed charge via Newton's third law.

toLevel5.question: An electron and a doubly-charged ion (charge +2e) are released from rest. The ion is 3680 times heavier than the electron. After a short time, how does the kinetic energy gained by the electron compare to that gained by the ion?
options: The electron gains 3680 times more kinetic energy
Both gain equal kinetic energy
The ion gains more kinetic energy because of its greater charge
The electron gains twice the kinetic energy

distractors.answer: Both gain equal kinetic energy
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — equal forces over equal time give equal impulse, so both have equal momentum. KE = p²/2m, so the lighter electron gains far more KE.

distractors.answer: The ion gains more kinetic energy because of its greater charge
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — charge affects force equally on both (Newton's third law); the lighter electron accelerates more and gains more KE.

distractors.answer: The electron gains twice the kinetic energy
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the ratio of kinetic energies equals the inverse mass ratio (3680 : 1), not 2 : 1.

toLevel5.question: A student argues: 'Because the electric force between a +Q and a +4Q charge is F = k(Q)(4Q)/r², the +Q charge feels a force of kQ²/r² and the +4Q charge feels a force of 4kQ²/r².' Evaluate this reasoning.
options: It is wrong; both charges experience the same force F = 4kQ²/r²
It is correct; each charge generates its own contribution to the force
It is wrong; the force on each charge is 2kQ²/r², split equally
It is partially correct; the net force lies between the two values

distractors.answer: It is correct; each charge generates its own contribution to the force
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Coulomb's law gives a single force magnitude F = kq₁q₂/r² that applies to both charges equally, as required by Newton's third law.

distractors.answer: It is wrong; the force on each charge is 2kQ²/r², split equally
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the force is not averaged between the charges; both experience the full force F = 4kQ²/r².

distractors.answer: It is partially correct; the net force lies between the two values
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — there is no intermediate force; both charges experience the identical magnitude F = 4kQ²/r².

toLevel5.question: Charges A (+3 μC, mass 1.0 g) and B (−6 μC, mass 4.0 g) are released from rest 0.05 m apart. What is the ratio of the initial acceleration of A to that of B?

distractors.explanation: Incorrect — this uses the charge ratio instead of the mass ratio; equal forces with mass ratio 1:4 gives acceleration ratio 4:1.
Incorrect — this inverts the relationship; the lighter charge has greater acceleration, giving a ratio of 4:1.
Incorrect — equal forces do not produce equal accelerations unless the masses are equal; here the mass ratio is 1:4.

toLevel5.question: Two charged particles interact electrically. If the charge on particle 1 is doubled and the charge on particle 2 is halved, how does the force on particle 1 change?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It halves
It quadruples

distractors.answer: It doubles
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the product q₁q₂ is unchanged (2q₁ × q₂/2 = q₁q₂), so the force remains the same; Newton's third law applies equally.

distractors.answer: It halves
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the product q₁q₂ is unchanged, so the force on both particles stays the same.

distractors.answer: It quadruples
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — only doubling both charges would quadruple the force; here one doubles and the other halves, keeping q₁q₂ constant.

toLevel5.question: In a hydrogen atom, the proton and electron attract each other. The electron orbits the proton rather than vice versa. Which explanation correctly uses Newton's third law?
options: Both experience equal forces, but the electron's much smaller mass gives it much greater acceleration
The proton exerts a stronger force on the electron because it is more massive
The electron exerts no force on the proton because it is so much lighter
The forces are equal only at specific orbital radii

distractors.answer: The proton exerts a stronger force on the electron because it is more massive
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — force magnitude is determined by charges and distance, not mass; Newton's third law ensures equal forces on both.

distractors.answer: The electron exerts no force on the proton because it is so much lighter
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law requires the electron to exert an equal and opposite force on the proton.

distractors.answer: The forces are equal only at specific orbital radii
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law forces are always equal in magnitude at any separation distance.

toLevel5.question: A Van de Graaff generator (charge +Q) repels a small pith ball (charge +q, where q << Q). A student observes the pith ball fly away while the generator remains stationary. Does this disprove Newton's third law?
options: No — equal forces produce very different accelerations when the masses are very different
Yes — the generator clearly exerts more force since it doesn't move
No — the generator doesn't experience any force from the pith ball
Yes — Newton's third law doesn't apply to charges of very different size

distractors.answer: Yes — the generator clearly exerts more force since it doesn't move
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — the generator barely moves because its mass is enormous; it still experiences the same magnitude of force as the pith ball.

distractors.answer: No — the generator doesn't experience any force from the pith ball
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law guarantees the pith ball exerts an equal force on the generator; the generator's large mass just makes its acceleration imperceptible.

distractors.answer: Yes — Newton's third law doesn't apply to charges of very different size
distractors.explanation: Incorrect — Newton's third law is universal and applies regardless of charge or mass differences.

toLevel5.question: When two unequal charges are released from rest, momentum is conserved because the forces form a Newton's third law pair. This means the total {{blank:1}} of the system remains {{blank:2}}.

A +Q charge and a +9Q charge repel each other. If +Q has mass m, the minimum mass of +9Q for it to have less than half the acceleration of +Q is any mass greater than {{blank:1}}. This is because a = F/m and both experience the {{blank:2}} force.
